TriO: Tri-Modal Unsupervised Occupancy
World Model for Anything Perception

Quinlan Sykora* Affiliation: Waabi Affiliation: University of Toronto, E-mail {qsykora,sbiswas,cdiehl,acunningham,tgilles,urtasun}@waabi.ai    Sourav Biswas* Affiliation: Waabi Affiliation: University of Toronto, E-mail {qsykora,sbiswas,cdiehl,acunningham,tgilles,urtasun}@waabi.ai    Christopher Diehl* Affiliation: Waabi    Andrew Cunningham Affiliation: Waabi    Thomas Gilles Affiliation: Waabi    Raquel Urtasun Affiliation: Waabi
Abstract

We present TriO, a multi-modal unsupervised world model that predicts 4D occupancy, obstacle segmentation, flow and LiDAR. In contrast to prior work, TriO utilizes three distinct sensor modalities (camera, LiDAR, and RADAR) as both inputs and sources of self-supervision, eliminating the need for additional human annotations. Thanks to its novel supervision, the model is able to segment any occupancy from the drivable surface, overcoming the limitations of existing open-set methods in handling long-tail objects. TriO achieves state-of-the-art results in multiple 3D and 4D tasks, including occupancy, flow, and LiDAR prediction, as well as zero-shot road obstacle segmentation across multiple datasets such as Argoverse 2, and Spotting the Unexpected.

1 Introduction

In order for a self-driving vehicle (SDV) to safely navigate through complex environments, it must first perceive anything, i.e. segment above ground obstacles from drivable areas at the current time, then forecast the evolution of the scene to plan its future motion. This problem has been predominantly tackled with object-based approaches [11, 53, 93, 92, 81, 35, 34, 13, 16, 10], which first detect objects and then forecast their future trajectories. In contrast, object-free occupancy approaches [62, 12, 80, 74, 31, 2, 17] overcome the downsides of thresholding detections and the limited representation capability of a finite set of trajectories.

However, most 3D/4D occupancy approaches [25, 61, 103, 26, 107] rely on dense voxel grid labels [85, 91] which are computationally expensive at high resolutions, and are constructed with human annotations (e.g., semantic LiDAR point annotations or bounding box labels). Due to the cost of the latter, and their difficulty to generate at scale, the volume of the labeled data is commonly orders of magnitude smaller than the amount of unlabeled data [1]. Moreover, the mentioned approaches are usually supervised with a finite set of semantic classes, which do not encapsulate safety-critical rare events.

Conversely, recent occupancy approaches [43, 1, 18] leverage LiDAR self-supervision, pre-training on vast amounts of sensor data and fine-tuning with a small amount of labeled data for downstream applications. However, LiDAR is susceptible to blooming [87], multipath returns [78], and limited range. Additional sensor modalities can be of benefit for self-supervised training, and multi-sensor fusion can increase robustness to sensor failures and adverse conditions.

Other methods have leveraged RGB cameras, either as inputs [71], distilling foundation model features [60], or predicting semantic pseudo-labels [54, 33, 48, 8, 22, 7] from camera-based models. Furthermore, many prior works [99, 97, 38, 76, 39] generate semantic labels with open-vocabulary segmentation models queried with text-prompts. However, common failure modes have been shown in open-set detectors [3] and segmentors [82], challenging their overall robustness to rare classes. Finally, the segmentation models require image-text pair annotations.

One generally overlooked modality is RADAR, which can enhance training by introducing radial velocity measurements, improve robustness under adverse weather conditions [49], and increase the observation range. While some works investigate RADAR-based 3D occupancy models using human annotations [20, 73], and others focus on RADAR-only input with self-supervision [46] or cross-modal LiDAR supervision [57], none integrate all aforementioned modalities in a unsupervised tri-modal 4D world model.

Motivated by these downsides, our goal is to develop a model that can leverage all three common sensor modalities (LiDAR, camera, and RADAR) as both input and supervision for occupancy in a self-supervised manner. Towards this goal, we propose TriO: a multi-modal world model that can predict and forecast 4D continuous occupancy, obstacle segmentation, and flow at any continuous (x,y,z,t)(x,y,z,t) coordinate from tri-modal observations. To achieve this, we leverage each sensor as both an input and as a unique form of supervision, ultimately combining the strengths of each modality to produce the best possible representation of the world. We further introduce a novel multi-sensor fusion architecture leading to better forecasting capabilities. Notably, being pre-trained on a vast amount of raw sensor data, TriO can be effectively leveraged for multiple downstream applications.

Historically, to determine which entities in the scene are relevant to the self-driving task, prior work uses semantic supervision from open-vocabulary models prompted with a closed set of multiple classes [99, 97, 38, 76, 39]. These however do not generalize to long tail events with rare obstacles, and hence do not cover all safety-critical scenarios. We argue the most general and robust requirement for occupancy is to semantically distinguish between what is occupied but not path-blocking (e.g., a flat surface that is traversable by the SDV) vs. occupied and path-blocking (e.g., a rare object on the road). Towards this end, we define the task of anything-perception as the ability to segment any object that exists above the road from the ground surface.

Despite demonstrating impressive open-set detection capabilities, the segmentation models of prior work used for 2D →\rightarrow 3D label distillation struggle to segment rare objects [82] (the long tail), even when prompted with the ground truth class, highlighting a lack of semantic understanding and generalization in current VLMs. To circumvent this, we propose a simple yet effective unsupervised11 1 We note that Metric3Dv2 [32] was partially trained on datasets with semi-supervised human annotations. In this context, we define unsupervised to mean not requiring direct human annotations. For more discussion refer to the supplementary. geometric image/LiDAR segmentation method that leverages representations from image depth model Metric3Dv2 [32], and the LiDAR segmentation heuristic from Patchwork++[47]. Our method detects any obstruction, leading to significant improvements in generalizable unknown object segmentation. Notably, in contrast to other vision-language based approaches which require at least textual image descriptions [76, 4, 39, 97, 86] or (semantic) mask labels [45, 99, 97, 38], our obstacle segmentation model relies solely on geometric properties rather than semantic annotations.

Contributions: 1) TriO uniquely uses all three common sensor modalities (camera, LiDAR, RADAR), both as input and for self-supervision. 2) We introduce a novel image/LiDAR-based obstacle segmentation technique that generates pseudo-labels for distillation into TriO, without requiring additional human labels in our training pipeline, while maintaining robustness and generalizability. 3) We propose a novel architecture fusing all modalities leading to better long-term forecasting. 4) TriO achieves state-of-the-art performance on a variety of tasks including point cloud forecasting, obstacle segmentation, and both 4D/3D occupancy and flow forecasting, validated on three real-world autonomous driving datasets (Argoverse2, Spotting the Unexpected, Long Range RADAR). Overall, the novelty of our contribution is the unique integration of all three sensor modalities as inputs, and as source of self-supervision for our output representations.

2 Related Work

Semantic Occupancy. The task of scene completion [66, 40, 98, 106] involves reconstructing a complete scene from sparse sensor measurements. Semantic scene completion [79, 14, 95, 5] further extends this by aiming to infer semantic classes for each completed region, a task closely related to semantic occupancy prediction. Contemporary methods in this domain [25, 61, 103, 26, 107] typically focus on predicting 3D or 4D occupancy voxel grids with their associated semantic labels. These approaches generally require dense voxel-level supervision [85, 91], which is often derived from costly human-annotated labels, such as 3D bounding boxes or semantic point clouds. More recently, several approaches [9, 100, 54, 7] have proposed distilling 2D pseudo-semantic labels from VLMs. However, these VLMs themselves rely on large-scale human annotations in the form of image-text pairs, and supervising with a closed set of classes inherently restricts generalization in open-world scenarios.
Anything Perception. Open-vocabulary segmentation methods perform classification via text prompts at inference time, overcoming the limitations of fixed, closed-set label spaces. In the 2D domain, two primary paradigms have emerged: one leverages open-set detectors like GroundingDINO [58] or OWLv2 [64] to prompt mask predictors such as SAM [45], while another [97, 38, 99] predicts mask proposals and classifies them by computing the similarity between mask embeddings and CLIP-style [75] text embeddings. These paradigms have been extended to the 3D domain through methods like SAL [69], which distills CLIP features for LiDAR segmentation. Similarly, recent open-vocabulary occupancy methods [90, 102, 37, 48] distill these features into voxel representations to enable open-world prompting. Despite their flexibility, these methods face two critical challenges: (1) they remain fundamentally dependent on models pre-trained on vast image-text and per-pixel mask annotations, and (2) they exhibit significant performance degradation for rare classes [82, 3]. In contrast, TriOs supervision relies on geometric cues from different sensors, enabling a more reliable segmentation of any object relative to the drivable surface. While ground segmentation has been extensively studied for LiDAR point clouds [70, 23, 47, 83], its application to occupancy remains limited. For example, [77] utilizes surface normals from stereo cameras and LiDAR to estimate ground regions in current time BEV (2D) occupancy maps, yet is constrained by the range of current measurements and segmentation networks that require pixel-level human annotations. In comparison, we distill fused obstacle segmentation estimates from LiDAR and monocular camera data and TriO has a unique ability of forecasting these segmentations in 4D.
Unsupervised Occupancy. Early non-learning-based methods [84, 68, 15] employed classical filtering techniques to estimate occupancy and flow without human annotations. With the advent of deep learning, 4D-Occ [43] proposed a LiDAR-only self-supervised approach to forecast 4D occupancy. However, its explicit 4D voxel grid representation suffers from significant memory and runtime inefficiencies, often forcing a trade-off between spatial resolution and reconstruction quality. To address these limitations, recent implicit occupancy methods [1, 60, 18, 54, 71] represent scenes in continuous space-time, leveraging self-supervision from LiDAR or camera inputs. Departing from implicit representations, SceneDino [36] predicts 3D geometry and feature fields from monocular input, achieving semantic scene completion through clustering and unsupervised distillation. Other recent works, such as [57], adopt cross-modal strategies using RADAR as input with LiDAR-based supervision. In contrast to all prior work, TriO utilizes camera, LiDAR, and RADAR data for both input and self-supervision, exploiting the inherent physical synergies between sensors to perform 4D forecasting of occupancy, segmentation, and flow. We show an extensive tabular comparison and further related works in the supplementary.

3 Unsupervised Multi-Modal Occupancy-Flow Method

To learn a robust representation of the world, we leverage the complementary physical properties of the standard SDV sensor suite: active sensors (LiDAR and RADAR) operating on Time-of-Flight principles, and passive cameras. While LiDAR provides high-precision 3D geometry capable of capturing free-space [1] and object surfaces [47], its sparse returns degrade at distance and in adverse weather. In contrast, RADAR uses longer wavelengths that penetrate fog and rain, and provide instantaneous radial velocity via the Doppler effect. Passive RGB cameras offer dense, high-resolution semantic and textural information, but lack native depth. To overcome this limitation, we extract dense depth and surface normal estimates using recent vision foundation models [32], enabling the reliable segmentation of obstacles. In summary, we combine the complementary synergies of each sensor modality and propose TriO, a 4D world model that learns geometry, dynamics, and object segmentation while remaining unsupervised.

3.1 Unsupervised Task

To define our training objective, let T∈ℕT\in\mathbb{N} denote the future time-horizon and H∈ℕH\in\mathbb{N} the historical observation time steps. For notational clarity, in the following we define 𝐒H=𝐒−H,…,0\mathbf{S}_{\text{H}}=\mathbf{S}_{-H,\dots,0} as the historical sensor observations at time −H,…,0-H,\dots,0 and 𝐒T\mathbf{S}_{\text{T}} as the future observations at time 0,…,T0,\dots,T. Here, 𝐒\mathbf{S} is a placeholder for either multi-view camera images 𝐂∈ℝNC×W×H×3\mathbf{C}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{\text{C}}\times W\times H\times 3}, LiDAR points 𝐋∈ℝNL×dL\mathbf{L}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{\text{L}}\times d_{\text{L}}}, or RADAR targets 𝐑∈ℝNR×dR\mathbf{R}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{\text{R}}\times d_{\text{R}}}. NCN_{\text{C}} denotes the number of camera images with width WW and height HH. Further, NLN_{\text{L}}, NRN_{\text{R}}, dLd_{\text{L}}, dRd_{\text{R}} are the number of LiDAR/RADAR points and their feature dimensionalities, respectively. Finally, we define the combined historical and future sensor observations as 𝐗H=(𝐂H,𝐋H,𝐑H)\mathbf{X}_{\text{H}}=(\mathbf{C}_{\text{H}},\mathbf{L}_{\text{H}},\mathbf{R}_{\text{H}}) and 𝐗T=(𝐂T,𝐋T,𝐑T)\mathbf{X}_{\text{T}}=(\mathbf{C}_{\text{T}},\mathbf{L}_{\text{T}},\mathbf{R}_{\text{T}}), respectively. Our goal is to learn a model:

𝐲=(o,s,𝐟)=fθ​(𝐗H,𝐪),\mathbf{y}=(o,s,\mathbf{f})=f_{\theta}(\mathbf{X}_{\text{H}},\mathbf{q}), (1)

parameterized by θ\theta, that can predict occupancy probability o∈[0,1]o\in[0,1], obstacle segmentation probability s∈[0,1]s\in[0,1] and 3D flow 𝐟∈ℝ3\mathbf{f}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} at query point 𝐪=(qx,qy,qz,qt)\mathbf{q}=(q_{x},q_{y},q_{z},q_{t}) in continuous 4D space-time (x,y,z,tx,y,z,t).

Geometric occupancy and 3D flow offer a simple representation that captures important characteristics of real-world environments (being occupied by a physical object and its velocity). However, a motion planner must distinguish between what is path-blocking (e.g., a child sitting on the street) and what is traversable (e.g., a drivable slope), motivating the prediction of obstacle segmentation ss. To train our method, we require labels for each query point 𝐪\mathbf{q}. We construct supervisory signals (pseudo-labels) as 𝐲¯=g⁡(𝐗T,𝐪)\bar{\mathbf{y}}=g(\mathbf{X}_{\text{T}},\mathbf{q}), which are used in the loss function ℒ⁡(𝐲,𝐲¯)\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{y},\bar{\mathbf{y}}).

In the remainder of this section, we first detail the architecture of fθf_{\theta} in Sec. 3.2. We then detail the function gg by introducing our segmentation method in Sec. 3.3 and how pseudo-labels are generated from all three sensor modalities in Sec. 3.4. The training procedure is described in Sec. 3.5.

3.2 Unsupervised Multi-Modal Occupancy-Flow Model

Our model follows an encoder-decoder structure and the overall architecture is shown in Fig. 2. First, we encode the measurements of each sensor with two encoders, one for LiDAR-RADAR (flrf_{\text{lr}}) and one for camera (fcf_{\text{c}}):

𝐙c=fc​(𝐂H),𝐙lr=flr​(𝐋H,𝐑H).\mathbf{Z}_{\text{c}}=f_{\text{c}}(\mathbf{C}_{\text{H}}),\quad\mathbf{Z}_{\text{lr}}=f_{\text{lr}}(\mathbf{L}_{\text{H}},\mathbf{R}_{\text{H}}). (2)

The camera encoder fcf_{\text{c}} is a pretrained version of ResNet50 [28], which only takes in the most recent camera frame. The LiDAR-RADAR encoder discretizes locations at the voxel level of multiple historical frames, and encodes them as features in a 3D sparse feature map. The features from the LiDAR 𝐥=[x,y,z,i,Δ​t]⊺∈ℝ5\mathbf{l}=[x,y,z,i,\Delta t]^{\intercal}\in\mathbb{R}^{5} (including intensity ii and relative timestep Δ​t\Delta t) and RADAR points 𝐫=[x,y,z,vr,σ,Δ​t]⊺∈ℝ6\mathbf{r}=[x,y,z,v_{r},\sigma,\Delta t]^{\intercal}\in\mathbb{R}^{6} (including range rate vrv_{r}, RADAR cross section σ\sigma, and Δ​t\Delta t) are each encoded through separate shallow MLPs.

The latent representations 𝐙c\mathbf{Z}_{\text{c}} and 𝐙lr\mathbf{Z}_{\text{lr}} are then fused by allowing the sparse LiDAR features at the coarsest level to attend to the image features through a voxel attention mechanism (fvoxelattf_{\text{voxelatt}}), similar to what is done in [52], giving 𝒵0=[𝐕2​x,𝐕4​x,𝐕8​x,𝐌16​x]\mathcal{Z}_{0}=[\mathbf{V}_{2x},\mathbf{V}_{4x},\mathbf{V}_{8x},\mathbf{M}_{16x}], with feature volumes 𝐕2​x,𝐕4​x,𝐕8​x\mathbf{V}_{2x},\mathbf{V}_{4x},\mathbf{V}_{8x} and 𝐌16​x\mathbf{M}_{16x} having been downsampled by 2x, 4x, 8x, and 16x respectively. We then densify the coarsest feature map 𝐌16​x\mathbf{M}_{16x} and pass it through several deformable attention layers (fdefattf_{\text{defatt}}) to increase the effective receptive field of the model. Finally, we use the same deformable attention multi-resolution header proposed by [18] for each of the model’s predictions. We describe the specific details in the supplementary. The process is summarized as:

𝒵0=fvoxelatt​(𝐙c,𝐙lr)→𝒵1=fdefatt​(𝒵0)→(o,𝐟,s)=fdec​(𝒵1,𝐙lr,𝐪).\mathcal{Z}_{0}=f_{\text{voxelatt}}(\mathbf{Z}_{\text{c}},\mathbf{Z}_{\text{lr}})\rightarrow\mathcal{Z}_{1}=f_{\text{defatt}}(\mathcal{Z}_{0})\rightarrow(o,\mathbf{f},s)=f_{\text{dec}}(\mathcal{Z}_{1},\mathbf{Z}_{\text{lr}},\mathbf{q}). (3)

3.3 Obstacle Segmentation Model

To provide supervision for obstacle segmentation ss, we propose a novel method for extracting obstacle/ground segmentation labels from image and LiDAR features in a probabilistic manner, combining the strength of each sensor modality. This approach ensures that the objects which are distinctly above ground are captured by the LiDAR segmentation, which is robust due to the 3D information it receives, while also detecting smaller close-to-the-ground obstacles that may only be observable in image space. The overall process is illustrated in Fig. 3.

Image Obstacle Segmentation. We propose using an image foundation model to produce estimates of normals and depths of the image for each camera. Specifically, given a camera image 𝐈∈ℝH×W×3\mathbf{I}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3} we apply Metric3Dv2 [32] to obtain per-pixel metric depth d∈ℝH×Wd\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W}, depth confidence c∈ℝH×Wc\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W}, and surface normals 𝐧^∈ℝH×W×3\hat{\mathbf{n}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3} with associated confidence cn∈ℝH×Wc_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W}. We then follow a similar process to [63] to produce a segmentation of the obstacles relative to the rest of the scene based on the normals and depth information. In contrast to prior work, which produce discrete labels, we output continuous probabilities for obstacles/ground (pobstimagep^{\text{image}}_{\text{obst}}), in addition to probabilities of the validity of the estimation (pvalidimagep^{\text{image}}_{\text{valid}}). Producing these continuous image segmentation labels (ISL) enables the downstream model to learn a more calibrated representation.
LiDAR Obstacle Segmentation. We leverage ideas from Patchwork++ [47] for LiDAR segmentation to discretize the point cloud into polar patches, where for each patch jj, a ground plane is characterized by its centroid 𝐜j∈ℝ3\mathbf{c}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} and surface normal 𝐧^j∈ℝ3\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}. For a LiDAR return 𝐥∈ℝ3\mathbf{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}, we identify its corresponding patch in the x​yxy-plane. We then get the elevation e∈ℝe\in\mathbb{R} as the point to plane distance using the patch normal, and map this into continuous probabilities for the obstacle pobstLiDARp^{\text{LiDAR}}_{\text{obst}} and the valid distribution pvalidLiDARp^{\text{LiDAR}}_{\text{valid}}.
Combined Segmentation. To leverage the complementary strengths of both modalities, we employ a confidence-driven fusion using the per-point validity and obstacle probabilities pvalidp_{\text{valid}}, pobstp_{\text{obst}} from both image (projected onto LiDAR) and LiDAR sources. Formally, the combined probability is

𝐩comb\displaystyle\mathbf{p}^{\text{comb}} ={𝐩image,if ​(pvalidLiDAR<0.5)∧(pvalidimage>pvalidLiDAR)𝐩LiDAR,otherwise\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\mathbf{p}^{\text{image}},&\text{if }(p^{\text{LiDAR}}_{\text{valid}}<0.5)\;\wedge\;(p^{\text{image}}_{\text{valid}}>p^{\text{LiDAR}}_{\text{valid}})\\ \mathbf{p}^{\text{LiDAR}},&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} (4)

with 𝐩source=[pvalidsource,pobstsource]⊺\mathbf{p}^{\textsc{source}}=\bigl[p^{\textsc{source}}_{\text{valid}},p^{\textsc{source}}_{\text{obst}}\bigr]^{\intercal}, source∈{comb,image,LiDAR}\textsc{source}\in\{\text{comb},\text{image},\,\text{LiDAR}\}. The probability vector 𝐩comb\mathbf{p}^{\text{comb}} describes the combined soft labels (CSL) to supervise ss. By prioritizing image labels for low-confidence LiDAR segmentation results, this approach captures small visual details while maintaining LiDAR’s robustness to points that are clearly distinct from the ground plane. Additional details of our segmentation method are in the supplementary.

3.4 Multi-Modal Self-Supervision

We will now outline the pseudo-labels used to supervise TriO. These can all be represented by a 4D query point 𝐪\mathbf{q}, and a label y¯\bar{y}, summarized as 𝐲¯=(𝐪,y¯)\bar{\mathbf{y}}=(\mathbf{q},\bar{y}).
Occupancy. We generate dense occupancy pseudo-labels without any human annotation, following the methodology of UnO [1], DIO [18], and GASP [60]. For a LiDAR return 𝐥\mathbf{l} we assume the continuous ray segment between the sensor position and 𝐥\mathbf{l} as the unoccupied region ℛ−\mathcal{R}^{-}, and a short segment immediately behind 𝐥\mathbf{l} along the ray direction as the occupied region ℛ+\mathcal{R}^{+}. The sets of occupied and unoccupied points in the scene are 𝒪+=⋃𝐥∈𝐋ℛ+\mathcal{O}^{+}=\bigcup_{\mathbf{l}\in\mathbf{L}}\mathcal{R}^{+} and 𝒪−=⋃𝐥∈𝐋ℛ−\mathcal{O}^{-}=\bigcup_{\mathbf{l}\in\mathbf{L}}\mathcal{R}^{-}, respectively. The set of 2​N2N sampled points with occupancy pseudo-labels is

𝒴occ\displaystyle\mathcal{Y}_{\text{occ}} ={(𝐪,1)∣𝐪∈𝒪+}∪{(𝐪,0)∣𝐪∈𝒪−}.\displaystyle=\{(\mathbf{q},1)\mid\mathbf{q}\in\mathcal{O}^{+}\}\cup\{(\mathbf{q},0)\mid\mathbf{q}\in\mathcal{O}^{-}\}. (5)

Obstacle Segmentation. In order to train for the segmentation class, we revisit the pseudo-labels generated in Sec. 3.3. Recall that this formulation provides a combined probability vector 𝐩comb\mathbf{p}^{\text{comb}} for each point 𝐫∈𝒫sweep\mathbf{r}\in\mathcal{P}_{\text{sweep}} in LiDAR sweep 𝒫sweep\mathcal{P}_{\text{sweep}}, containing both the validity and obstacle probabilities. We therefore use the locations of these LiDAR points with their time of emission (x,y,z,tx,y,z,t) as coordinates for our query 𝐪\mathbf{q}, and their corresponding combined probabilities as the soft labels. The set of points with pseudo-labels 𝒴seg\mathcal{Y}_{\text{seg}} is

𝒴seg={(𝐪,𝐩comb​(𝐪))∣𝐪∈𝒫sweep}.\mathcal{Y}_{\text{seg}}=\{(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{p}^{\text{comb}}(\mathbf{q}))\mid\mathbf{q}\in\mathcal{P}_{\text{sweep}}\}. (6)

Instantaneous Flow. In order to train for unsupervised instantaneous flow, we use the Doppler readings from the RADAR sensor as our supervision source. As RADAR points can be noisy, we first define a refined set of RADAR points ℛclean\mathcal{R}_{\text{clean}} where the measurement uncertainty is below a certain threshold. Due to the inherent characteristic that RADAR only captures velocity in the radial direction, our pseudo-labels must include the sensor velocity at the time of measurement 𝐯sensor\mathbf{v}_{\text{sensor}}, the unit radial direction of the RADAR point 𝐝radar\mathbf{d}_{\text{radar}}, and the scalar Doppler velocity vdopplerv_{\text{doppler}}. We define the flow pseudo-label set 𝒴flow\mathcal{Y}_{\text{flow}} as:

𝒴flow={(𝐪,(vdoppler,𝐯sensor,𝐝radar))∣𝐪∈ℛclean}.\mathcal{Y}_{\text{flow}}=\{(\mathbf{q},(v_{\text{doppler}},\mathbf{v}_{\text{sensor}},\mathbf{d}_{\text{radar}}))\mid\mathbf{q}\in\mathcal{R}_{\text{clean}}\}. (7)

3.5 Training

We train our model with a multi-task loss for occupancy (ℒocc\mathcal{L}_{\text{occ}}), flow (ℒflow\mathcal{L}_{\text{flow}}), and obstacle probability (ℒseg\mathcal{L}_{\text{seg}})

ℒ=λ1​ℒocc+λ2​ℒflow+λ3​ℒseg\mathcal{L}=\lambda_{1}\mathcal{L}_{\text{occ}}+\lambda_{2}\mathcal{L}_{\text{flow}}+\lambda_{3}\mathcal{L}_{\text{seg}} (8)

using the pseudo-labels defined by 𝒴occ\mathcal{Y}_{\text{occ}}, 𝒴seg\mathcal{Y}_{\text{seg}}, and 𝒴flow\mathcal{Y}_{\text{flow}}. Let TriO’s occupancy, obstacle probability, and flow output at a query point 𝐪\mathbf{q} be denoted as fθ,occ​(𝐪)∈[0,1]f_{\theta,\text{occ}}(\mathbf{q})\in[0,1], fθ,seg​(𝐪)∈[0,1]f_{\theta,\text{seg}}(\mathbf{q})\in[0,1], and fθ,flow​(𝐪)∈ℝ3f_{\theta,\text{flow}}(\mathbf{q})\in\mathbb{R}^{3} respectively. For notational simplicity, we drop the conditioning on the input 𝐗H\mathbf{X}_{\text{H}}. The occupancy loss is the binary cross-entropy loss over all query points:

ℒocc\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{occ}} =1|𝒴occ|​∑(𝐪,y¯occ)∈𝒴occBCE​(fθ,occ​(𝐪),y¯occ).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Y}_{\text{occ}}|}\sum_{(\mathbf{q},\bar{y}_{\text{occ}})\in\mathcal{Y}_{\text{occ}}}\text{BCE}\left(f_{\theta,\text{occ}}(\mathbf{q}),\;\bar{y}_{\text{occ}}\right). (9)

The obstacle probability loss is a soft focal loss (SFocalLoss):

ℒseg\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{seg}} =1|𝒴seg|​∑(𝐪,pcomb​(𝐪))∈𝒴segSFocalLoss​(fθ,seg​(𝐪),pobstcomb​(𝐪),pvalidcomb​(𝐪)).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Y}_{\text{seg}}|}\sum_{(\mathbf{q},p^{\text{comb}}(\mathbf{q}))\in\mathcal{Y}_{\text{seg}}}\text{SFocalLoss}\left(f_{\theta,\text{seg}}(\mathbf{q}),\;p^{\text{comb}}_{\text{obst}}(\mathbf{q}),\;p^{\text{comb}}_{\text{valid}}(\mathbf{q})\right). (10)

In contrast to ℒocc\mathcal{L}_{\text{occ}}, which uses hard labels y¯occ∈{0,1}\bar{y}_{\text{occ}}\in\{0,1\}, ℒseg\mathcal{L}_{\text{seg}} operates on soft targets pobstcomb∈[0,1]p^{\text{comb}}_{\text{obst}}\in[0,1], with each point’s contribution scaled by its label confidence pvalidcombp^{\text{comb}}_{\text{valid}}. We find this soft parameterization to be important for generating a well-calibrated model and elaborate further in Sec. 4. Full loss definitions are provided in the supplementary material. Finally, the flow supervision is determined as follows. We begin by moving the model’s instantaneous 3D flow prediction fθ,flow​(𝐪)f_{\theta,\text{flow}}(\mathbf{q}) into the sensor’s frame of reference by subtracting the sensor’s velocity 𝐯sensor\mathbf{v}_{\text{sensor}}, yielding the relative flow 𝐟rel​(𝐪)=fθ,flow​(𝐪)−𝐯sensor\mathbf{f}_{\text{rel}}(\mathbf{q})=f_{\theta,\text{flow}}(\mathbf{q})-\mathbf{v}_{\text{sensor}}. We then project this relative flow onto the radial direction vector 𝐝radar\mathbf{d}_{\text{radar}} to obtain the predicted radial velocity: frad​(𝐪)=𝐝radar⋅𝐟rel​(𝐪)f_{\text{rad}}(\mathbf{q})=\mathbf{d}_{\text{radar}}\cdot\mathbf{f}_{\text{rel}}(\mathbf{q}). Finally, we supervise this value using the Doppler measurements with an L1L_{1} loss over the cleaned RADAR points ℛclean\mathcal{R}_{\text{clean}}:

ℒflow=1|ℛclean|​∑𝐪∈ℛclean|frad​(𝐪)−vdoppler|.\mathcal{L}_{\text{flow}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}_{\text{clean}}|}\sum_{\mathbf{q}\in\mathcal{R}_{\text{clean}}}\left|f_{\text{rad}}(\mathbf{q})-v_{\text{doppler}}\right|. (11)

4 Experiments

In this section, we investigate the following research questions while comparing against the state-of-the-art: Q1: Can TriO reliably perceive unknown objects in a zero-shot, open-set manner? Q2: Does TriO’s architecture lead to a better 4D geometric representation? Q3: Does unsupervised multi-modal pre-training improve downstream task performance via fine-tuning?
Datasets. We use the Argoverse 2 (AV2) [94] Sensor split (700 train/ 150 val sequences) and evaluate on the AV2 Occupancy Forecasting leaderboard. The dataset Spotting the Unexpected (STU) [67] uniquely provides 3D LiDAR point labels for rarely seen objects on the road, aiming to test models on anything perception. We utilize all 22 available sequences with labels from STU (train and val) for evaluation. Note, STU is only for zero-shot evaluation – i.e. we train TriO and baselines on AV2 and apply it without any fine-tuning on STU, containing different sensor characteristics. Given the limited label range and no RADAR in previous datasets, we use an unreleased dataset Long Range RADAR (LRR) where we label bounding boxes up to 350m in front of the SDV. LRR has 2280 sequences (highway and urban). See supplementary for details.

4.1 Zero-Shot Anything Perception (Q1)

We evaluate our method’s ability to perceive unusual, path-blocking objects on STU. First, we assess pseudo-label quality by comparing our ISL and CSL against STU ground truth. Using the correspondence between image and LiDAR labels in STU, we benchmark our soft pseudo-labels against open-set 2D and 3D baselines on equal footing. We also provide qualitatives results on AV2 in Fig. 4.

Anything Perception Baselines. We benchmark against state-of-the-art open-vocabulary methods, including detect-then-segment (GroundedSAM [76], OWLv2 [64]+SAM [45]) and segment-then-classify (MaskCLIP++ [99] with FC-CLIP [97], MAFT+ [38], or SAM) approaches. Following [69], we use standard prompts for ground (𝒫ground\mathcal{P}_{\text{ground}}) and non-ground (𝒫obstacle\mathcal{P}_{\text{obstacle}}) classes; see supplementary material for details. To establish an upper performance bound, we include an (Oracle) variant where scenes are manually inspected and specific unknown object classes are appended to 𝒫obstacle\mathcal{P}_{\text{obstacle}}. Finally, we also include Patchwork++ [47] as a LiDAR-based baseline. For the second set of experiments, we train TriO’s segmentation objective (ℒseg\mathcal{L}_{\text{seg}}) using each of the pseudo-label from the baselines. This allows us to measure how effectively open-world knowledge can be distilled into the downstream world model, and in turn how well this model generalizes when evaluated on a different domain. Notably, our model under GroundedSAM supervision serves as a LiDAR-enhanced version of QueryOcc+ [54]. Finally, we compare against LiDAR-only models (UnO, DiO) trained with ISL and CSL.

Anything Perception Metrics. We report mIoU (mean Intersection over Union) [85, 91] for semantic predictions and F1 score to evaluate pseudo-label quality at a fixed operating point without unfairly advantaging soft probability methods. We emphasize Recall to capture safety-critical missed detections, while Average Precision (AP) evaluates continuous probabilities in distilled occupancy models. See supplementary for further details.
Comparison of Pseudo-Label Methods. Our generated pseudo-labels (CSL) achieve the best balance of detecting the obstacles (measured by recall) on the road without too many false positive detections (F1 and mIoU) as shown in Tab. 2. Notably, this strong performance is not solely reliant on multi-modal fusion; even our image-only pseudo-labels (ISL) surpass all evaluated baselines in terms of recall. We also find that text-based segmentation baselines, even when prompted with the exact text description of the objects in the road, struggle to generalize to these rarely seen classes, reinforcing the findings of [82]. We provide visual evidence for that claim in Fig. 5 and the supplementary. In contrast, our model, relying on geometry, is able to generalize in a more robust manner.
Semantic Occupancy Evaluation. As shown in Tab. 2 TriO performs the best after the obstacle labels have been distilled into our occupancy model. We also find that using soft probabilistic labels (CSL Soft) tends to result in better performance than when trained with thresholded discretized labels (CSL Hard) due to better calibration (see AP, mIoU). TriO improves also over LiDAR-only methods highlighting the benefit of using multi-modal sensor information.

4.2 Geometric Occupancy/ LiDAR Point Cloud Forecasting (Q2)

We evaluate TriO on the AV2 Occupancy Forecasting benchmark; the goal of this benchmark is to determine how TriO performs on occupancy prediction (visualized in Fig. 6), evaluated via LiDAR point cloud forecasting. Following prior work [43, 1, 18], after training the world model fθf_{\theta}, we freeze all parameters θ\theta and introduce a LiDAR forecasting header fψf_{\psi} to predict LiDAR depth. We provide more details in the supplementary.
LiDAR Forecasting Baselines. We compare our method against the state-of-the-art from the Argoverse 2 leaderboard. Notably, 4D-Occ [43] serves as a representative unsupervised baseline for explicit occupancy prediction via voxel grid forecasting. In contrast, UnO [1] and DiO [18], also perform implicit occupancy prediction. However, unlike TriO, these methods do not incorporate camera input, representing architectural differences in sensor modality.
LiDAR Forecasting Metrics: For point cloud forecasting we use well-established metrics of the AV2 Occupancy Forecasting leaderboard, namely Chamfer distance (CD), Near Field Chamfer Distance (NFCD), depth L1 error (L1), depth relative L1 error (AbsRel) as our metrics.
Comparison against state-of-the-art. Tab. 3 compares TriO against all the AV2 leaderboard baselines. TriO is best in the L1 and AbsRel metrics, while competitive with baselines in other metrics. This underlines TriO’s ability to accurately forecast occupancy and its effectiveness as a world model.

4.3 Fine-tuning for Downstream Occupancy Tasks (Q3)

We show the versatility of the TriO pre-trained feature extractor by evaluating its performance on various downstream tasks. We follow [60, 1] and finetune the model to forecast semantic 3D (AV2) and semantic 2D BEV (LRR) occupancy and flow over time supervised with bounding box labels for the vehicle class.
Downstream Occupancy Baselines. For fine-tuning experiments, we pre-train UnO and DiO baselines via LiDAR self-supervision then fine-tune on 2D or 3D bounding box labels. We also compare against ImplicitO [2] which does not utilize unsupervised pre-training.
Downstream Occupancy Metrics. We use well-established metrics to evaluate the performance of the different methods on these downstream tasks by following prior work [62, 2, 1, 18]. We report mAP, SoftIoU [62] for occupancy and End Point Error (EPE) for flow. For LRR, we also evaluate each metric at over 200m in front of the SDV. We hypothesize that RADAR specifically having a longer effective range is able to improve our model performance at these distances, where other sensor readings may be too sparse to be consistently useful. This emphasizes the use case of LRR as only it is able to provide validation labels at a distance of 350m in front of the SDV.
Semantic Occupancy and Flow Forecasting. Tab. 4 and Tab. 5 show the BEV and 3D occupancy and flow forecasting results on AV2 and LRR. Our method outperforms all the baselines when finetuned to the supervised occupancy task. The drop in EPE performance in Tab. 4 compared to DIO is explained as TriO on AV2 has no flow supervision (due to the absence of RADAR data) during pre-training, whereas DIO does. Notably, our model outperforms the baselines significantly at range. The results show an improvement of 6.4 AP over the state-of-the-art showcasing the benefits of using RADAR at long-range.
Ablation Study. We evaluate the contributions of pre-training, sensor modalities, and loss objectives in Tab. 5. Unsupervised pre-training provides consistent gains across all metrics, validating the world model objectives. Omitting the radar loss leads to degradation in flow metrics across all ranges. Conversely, adding camera inputs improves far range occupancy performance at the expense of EPE; this suggests that single-frame camera features, which lack temporal context, may introduce noise into the flow estimation process. Removing RADAR as an input modality significantly degrades performance on long range metrics, supporting our hypothesis that this sensor modality directly lends itself to long range tasks.
Scaling Labeled Data. In Fig. 7 we scale the number of labeled training samples when fine-tuning pre-trained models (TriO, UnO, DIO) and models trained from scratch (ImplicitO-4D). TriO outperforms at all levels of supervision, and with 10210^{2} labeled training examples, reaches similar performance to the strongest baselines with 10410^{4} examples. TriO is two-orders of magnitude more sample efficient, underscoring the generalizability of our method. Due to its novel obstacle segmentation supervision TriO better understands obstacles and free space. This underlines the strong representation learned during pre-training and TriO’s ability to encode the geometry, semantics, and dynamics of the scene.

Limitations, Discussion, and Future Work.

Currently, TriO is limited to using RADAR for flow self-supervision, but future work could add occupancy supervision from RADAR. While our model uses RADAR to generalize occupancy predictions beyond the LiDAR range, RADAR can also be used as additional occupancy supervision in adverse weather to robustify predictions. This requires techniques beyond the line-of-sight assumption done in [46] due to nature of RADAR returns. Furthermore, the ability to perceive and forecast the movement of rare objects is an understudied problem in the SDV space. We see a general need for additional larger scale benchmarks focusing on the task of Anything Perception to ensure the overall robustness of many pre-existing systems.

5 Conclusion

We present TriO, a novel unsupervised tri-modal occupancy model that learns to predict 4D occupancy, obstacle semantics, and flow by leveraging the complementary physical synergies of camera, LiDAR, and RADAR data. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple tasks, including zero-shot anything perception, LiDAR forecasting, and 3D/4D occupancy prediction, while being unsupervised and independent of additional costly human annotations. We observe failure-cases of open-vocabulary methods for rare classes, and show that TriO outperforms these methods in open-world scenarios. Notably, it achieves robust performance in perceiving anything relative to the drivable surface, including rare classes, showcasing its potential for a scalable deployment of SDVs.

Supplementary Materials
TriO: Tri-Modal Unsupervised Occupancy World Model for Anything Perception

This supplementary material provides additional related work, implementation details, the experimental setup, and further results.

Contents

A Extended Related Works

This section provides an additional comparison to related work. We begin by revisiting occupancy-related approaches described in the main paper. Tab. 6 compares the most closely related methods in terms of input modalities, supervision signals, and model properties. TriO is the only method that uses all three modalities for both input and self-supervision, while remaining unsupervised and modeling continuous occupancy in 4D.

Self-Supervised Flow Predictions.

TriO is also related to self-supervised scene flow methods, which can be grouped into two categories. The first solves global optimization problems using test-time optimization techniques to estimate point flow across multiple frames [89, 51]. One downside of this approach is its high runtime, which often makes these methods unsuitable for real-time applications. The second category uses feed-forward neural networks to predict point flow across frames. This is achieved through self-supervised losses [50, 101, 56, 44, 30] or distillation from test-time optimization techniques [88]. The previously mentioned methods primarily rely on multiple frames of LiDAR point cloud data. However, RADAR data can provide a partial supervision signal for velocity estimation via the Doppler effect. For example, [19] uses RADAR data, including radial velocity measurements from 4D RADARs. Other methods also combine occupancy and flow estimation: [18] proposes a occupancy consistency loss between 3D occupancy predictions to infer flow while relying solely on LiDAR. [59] estimates 3D occupancy and occupancy flow using only camera inputs, with self-supervision via differentiable rendering.

In contrast, our method is not only able to predict 4D occupancy and obstacle segmentations, but also uniquely combines multiple sensor modalities as input and self-supervised flow learning with RADAR velocity, while additionally predicting future 4D flow.

Pre-Training for Perception.

Representation learning methods aim to leverage large-scale unlabeled data to enhance performance on downstream tasks. Beyond the occupancy-based approaches [43, 1, 60, 18, 71, 54], which utilize LiDAR or camera self-supervision, several general-purpose representation learning frameworks have emerged. For instance, VoxelMAE [29] employs masked auto-encoding on voxelized point clouds as an effective pre-training strategy for 3D object detection. UniPAD [96] integrates both camera and LiDAR inputs within a 3D differentiable rendering framework to reconstruct color and depth. More recently, AD-L-JEPA [104] introduced a Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) for LiDAR, demonstrating superior downstream detection performance compared to traditional generative masked auto-encoders. In the RADAR domain, RaDICaL [27] proposed RADAR-to-RADAR and RADAR-to-VISION contrastive losses as a self-supervised pre-training objective. LEROjD [72] introduces a LIDAR-to-RADAR cross-modal distillation and LiDAR thin-out strategies for downstream RADAR-only object detection.

In contrast to these single- or dual-modality approaches, TriO utilizes pre-training across all three modalities simultaneously. Furthermore, while existing methods focus primarily on representations for instantaneous downstream tasks (e.g. detection), TriO specifically targets representations optimized for temporal 4D forecasting.

B Implementation Details

B.1 Network Architecture

In this subsection we revisit the architecture of TriO and provide additional details on the implementation.

Encoder:

We instantiate the camera encoder fcf_{\text{c}} as a ResNet50 [28] operating on NCN_{C} input images 𝐂\mathbf{C} of size 1920×10801920\times 1080. The LiDAR-RADAR branch voxelizes the multi-frame point measurements and encodes them into a sparse 3D feature grid. The voxel ROI spans [−50,350][-50,350] m along the longitudinal axis, [−50,50][-50,50] m along the lateral axis, both with a resolution of 0.156250.15625m, and [−2,4][-2,4] m in the vertical dimension, with a height resolution of 0.20.2m. Beyond spatial coordinates relative to the center of their corresponding voxel cell, (x,y,z)r∈ℝ3(x,y,z)_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}, the features from the LiDAR points 𝐥=[x,y,z,i,Δ​t]⊺∈ℝ5\mathbf{l}=[x,y,z,i,\Delta t]^{\intercal}\in\mathbb{R}^{5} (including intensity ii and relative timestep Δ​t\Delta t) and RADAR points 𝐫=[x,y,z,vr,σ,Δ​t]⊺∈ℝ6\mathbf{r}=[x,y,z,v_{r},\sigma,\Delta t]^{\intercal}\in\mathbb{R}^{6} (including range rate vrv_{r}, RCS σ\sigma, and Δ​t\Delta t) are passed through separate two-layer MLPs with group norm to encode the input features of dimension 5 or 6 outputting features of size 15. The LiDAR intensity is rasterized in BEV and concatenated such that the final output has size 16. We aggregate points in the same voxel with mean aggregation. The result is a sparse feature grid 𝐙voxel∈ℝ30×640×2560\mathbf{Z}_{\text{voxel}}\in\mathbb{R}^{30\times 640\times 2560}. This tensor is passed through a series of sparse convolutions (LiDAR-RADAR backbone) [24] progressively halving the spatial resolution and doubling the channel dimension (16→\to32→\to64→\to128 channels), yielding 𝐙lr∈ℝ320×80×4×128\mathbf{Z}_{\text{lr}}\in\mathbb{R}^{320\times 80\times 4\times 128} at 8×8{\times} spatial downsampling, which is ultimately fused with the image features 𝐙c\mathbf{Z}_{\text{c}}.

Feature Fusion.

In order to fuse the features from the RADAR-LiDAR encoder and the image encoder 𝐙c,𝐙lr\mathbf{Z}_{\text{c}},\mathbf{Z}_{\text{lr}}, we employ an image to sparse voxel attention mechanism, inspired by [52] giving 𝒵0=[𝐕2​x,𝐕4​x,𝐕8​x,𝐌16​x]\mathcal{Z}_{0}=[\mathbf{V}_{2x},\mathbf{V}_{4x},\mathbf{V}_{8x},\mathbf{M}_{16x}], with feature volumes 𝐕2​x,𝐕4​x,𝐕8​x\mathbf{V}_{2x},\mathbf{V}_{4x},\mathbf{V}_{8x} and BEV feature map 𝐌16​x\mathbf{M}_{16x} having resolution downsampled by 2x, 4x, 8x, and 16x, respectively:

𝒵0=fvoxelatt​(𝐙c,𝐙lr)\mathcal{Z}_{0}=f_{\text{voxelatt}}(\mathbf{Z}_{\text{c}},\mathbf{Z}_{\text{lr}}) (12)

However, in our implementation, we allow each of the sparse features to attend using deformable attention back into the image features, using their projected location in image space as the center of the deformable attention mechanism. We also encode the position features in both the LiDAR and image space before running through the attention mechanism. 𝐙c∈ℝNcam×128×Hc×Wc\mathbf{Z}_{\text{c}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{\text{cam}}\times 128\times H_{c}\times W_{c}} denotes the camera feature maps from the ResNet50 image backbone, and 𝐌16​x∈ℝ256×80×320\mathbf{M}_{16x}\in\mathbb{R}^{256\times 80\times 320} is the resulting fused dense BEV feature map. We then get 𝒵0\mathcal{Z}_{0} by using 𝐌16​x\mathbf{M}_{16x} and the intermediate feature maps of the previously mentioned LiDAR-RADAR backbone.

Deformable Attention Neck.

The fused BEV feature map 𝒵0\mathcal{Z}_{0} is passed through a multi-scale neck fdeformattf_{\text{deformatt}} composed of a ResNet with deformable convolution blocks [105] followed by a feature pyramid network (FPN) [55], yielding:

𝒵1=fdeformatt​(𝒵0).\mathcal{Z}_{1}=f_{\text{deformatt}}(\mathcal{Z}_{0}). (13)

Each deformable convolution block learns offsets, enabling the network to adaptively expand its receptive field beyond the fixed local neighborhood of standard convolutions. The FPN aggregates these features producing a rich BEV representation at the original spatial resolution of 𝐌16​x\mathbf{M}_{16x}. This is reminiscent of what is done in DIO [18], but with the additional deformable convolution operations enabling larger effective receptive fields, resulting in better forecasting of fast-moving entities.

Decoder.

For the decoder fdecf_{\text{dec}}, we use the multiscale deformable attention mechanism of [18],

(o,𝐟,s)=fdec​(𝒵1,𝐙lr,𝐪).(o,\mathbf{f},s)=f_{\text{dec}}(\mathcal{Z}_{1},\mathbf{Z}_{\text{lr}},\mathbf{q}). (14)

Specifically, given a query point 𝐪\mathbf{q}, the header attends to each level of the sparse feature maps (𝐕2​x,𝐕4​x,𝐕8​x\mathbf{V}_{2x},\mathbf{V}_{4x},\mathbf{V}_{8x}) and the dense feature map in 𝒵1\mathcal{Z}_{1} at the location of this query point in 3D space. We then perform deformable attention to attend to a series of different locations, querying each of them across all feature maps, and combining them using the same deformable attention mechanism. The final features are then passed through a shallow MLP which decodes the occupancy probability oo, the instantaneous motion (flow) 𝐟\mathbf{f} of the point, and the probability ss of that point being classified as an obstacle. This operation can be done efficiently in parallel for a batch of query points.

B.2 Obstacle Segmentation Model

This section provides implementation details of the obstacle segmentation pipeline used to supervise ss, including the per-modality pseudo-label construction and fusion rule.

Image Obstacle Segmentation.

For each camera image 𝐈∈ℝH×W×3\mathbf{I}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3} with known intrinsics K∈ℝ3×3K\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3} and extrinsic pose Tcam→vehT_{\text{cam}\to\text{veh}}, we use Metric3D v2 [32] to obtain per-pixel metric depth d∈ℝH×Wd\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W}, depth confidence c∈ℝH×Wc\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W}, and surface normals 𝐧^∈ℝH×W×3\hat{\mathbf{n}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3} with associated confidence cn∈ℝH×Wc_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W}.

We then convert each pixel to a 3D point and transform it, together with the normals, into vehicle frame. Let 𝐩\mathbf{p} and 𝐧\mathbf{n} denote a resulting 3D point and surface normal vector, respectively. On a high-level we assume that obstacle regions are defined by points with upwards (in zz) pointing normals and smooth normal gradients.

Soft Probabilistic Obstacle Criteria. Rather than applying hard thresholds we convert each geometric criterion into a soft probability using a parameterized sigmoid:

στ,k​(x)=1−1+e−k​τ1+ek⁡(x−τ),\sigma_{\tau,k}(x)=1-\frac{1+e^{-k\tau}}{1+e^{k(x-\tau)}}, (15)

where τ\tau is the transition point and kk controls the steepness. This function transitions smoothly from 00 at x=0x{=}0 to ≈1{\approx}1 for x≫τx\gg\tau. For criteria where high values indicate invalidity, we use the complement σ¯τ,k​(x)=1−στ,k​(x)\bar{\sigma}_{\tau,k}(x)=1-\sigma_{\tau,k}(x). We compute four independent per-pixel probabilities:

  1. 1.

    Normal orientation: pnorm=στn,kn​(nz)p_{\text{norm}}=\sigma_{\tau_{n},k_{n}}(n_{z}), assigning high probability to upward-facing surfaces.

  2. 2.

    Normal smoothness: pgrad=σ¯τg,kg​(∥∇𝐧∥)p_{\text{grad}}=\bar{\sigma}_{\tau_{g},k_{g}}\!\bigl(\lVert\nabla\,\mathbf{n}\rVert\bigr), where ∥∇𝐧∥\lVert\nabla\,\mathbf{n}\rVert is the normalized spatial image gradient of the normal field. We assume ground regions exhibit spatially smooth normals, while object boundaries produce large normalized gradients.

  3. 3.

    Depth confidence: pconf=στc,kc​(c)p_{\text{conf}}=\sigma_{\tau_{c},k_{c}}(c), assigning low probability for points where depth estimates are unconfident.

  4. 4.

    Range: pdist=σ¯τd,kd​(px)p_{\text{dist}}=\bar{\sigma}_{\tau_{d},k_{d}}(p_{x}), assigning low probability for distant points where monocular depth degrades.

RANSAC Plane Refinement. To further disambiguate ground from elevated flat surfaces (e.g., vehicle rooftops), we fit a ground plane to candidate 3D points using RANSAC [21]. We select candidate ground points as those whose combined probability exceeds a threshold τπ\tau_{\pi}:

pconf⋅pdist⋅pnorm⋅pgrad>τπ.p_{\text{conf}}\cdot p_{\text{dist}}\cdot p_{\text{norm}}\cdot p_{\text{grad}}>\tau_{\pi}. (16)

After applying RANSAC we compute the point-to-plane distance dplaned_{\text{plane}}, and the soft probability:

pplane=σ¯τr,kr​(dplane).p_{\text{plane}}=\bar{\sigma}_{\tau_{r},k_{r}}\left(d_{\text{plane}}\right). (17)

Final Obstacle and Validity Probabilities. We define the ground probability as the product of the normal-based criteria, and the obstacle probability as the inverse

pground=pnorm⋅pgrad\displaystyle p_{\text{ground}}=p_{\text{norm}}\cdot p_{\text{grad}} (18)
pobst=1−pground\displaystyle p_{\text{obst}}=1-p_{\text{ground}} (19)

and the validity probability, which captures whether a pixel carries reliable geometric information or belong to regions like the sky:

pvalid=σ⁡(cn)⋅pconf⋅pdist⋅(1−(1−pplane)⋅pground),p_{\text{valid}}=\sigma(c_{n})\cdot p_{\text{conf}}\cdot p_{\text{dist}}\cdot\bigl(1-(1-p_{\text{plane}})\cdot p_{\text{ground}}\bigr), (20)

where σ⁡(cn)\sigma(c_{n}) is the standard sigmoid of the normal confidence.

The resulting per-pixel distribution over three classes is:

pinvalidimage\displaystyle p^{\text{image}}_{\text{invalid}} =1−pvalid,\displaystyle=1-p_{\text{valid}}, (21)
pobstimage\displaystyle p^{\text{image}}_{\text{obst}} =pvalid⋅(1−pground),\displaystyle=p_{\text{valid}}\cdot(1-p_{\text{ground}}), (22)
pgroundimage\displaystyle p^{\text{image}}_{\text{ground}} =pvalid⋅pground.\displaystyle=p_{\text{valid}}\cdot p_{\text{ground}}. (23)

These soft image-space labels (ISL) are projected onto 3D LiDAR points via camera–LiDAR calibration to produce dense supervisory signals for the model output ss. The output is a set of LiDAR points with confidences and their probability of being associated with the ground class, defined by pvalidimagep^{\text{image}}_{\text{valid}} and pgroundimagep^{\text{image}}_{\text{ground}}, respectively.

LiDAR Obstacle Segmentation.

We take inspiration from Patchwork++ [47]; however, rather than using its final obstacle segmentation output, we utilize its core ideas for local ground patch estimation. We first discretize the point cloud into polar patches, where for each patch jj, a ground plane is characterized by its centroid 𝐜j∈ℝ3\mathbf{c}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} and surface normal 𝐧^j∈ℝ3\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}. For a LiDAR return 𝐥∈ℝ3\mathbf{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}, we identify its corresponding patch in the x​yxy-plane. We then get the elevation e∈ℝe\in\mathbb{R} as the point to plane distance using the patch normal, which we finally convert into a probability using a parametrized sigmoid

pobstLiDAR=στe,ke​(ei),p^{\text{LiDAR}}_{\text{obst}}=\sigma_{\tau_{e},k_{e}}(e_{i}), (24)

To define the validity probability, we quantify the uncertainty of the obstacle classification using a scaled binary entropy ℋ\mathcal{H}. This ensures that points with ambiguous geometric features contribute less to the supervisory signal. The LiDAR validity is

pvalidLiDAR=−λ​ℋ​(pobstLiDAR)+γ,p^{\text{LiDAR}}_{\text{valid}}=-\lambda\mathcal{H}(p^{\text{LiDAR}}_{\text{obst}})+\gamma, (25)

where λ\lambda and γ\gamma scale this to range between 0 and 1, ensuring that a probability of 0.5 results in a low validity score. This provides us with the LiDAR segmentation probabilities.

Fused Obstacle Segmentation.

We use a confidence-based fusion rule to select the supervision source per LiDAR point from the image or LiDAR based segmentation. Specifically, if the LiDAR segmentation validity is low and the image validity is higher, we use image labels; otherwise, we keep LiDAR labels:

𝐩comb\displaystyle\mathbf{p}^{\text{comb}} ={𝐩image,if ​pvalidLiDAR<0.5∧pvalidimage>pvalidLiDAR𝐩LiDAR,otherwise\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\mathbf{p}^{\text{image}},&\text{if }p^{\text{LiDAR}}_{\text{valid}}<0.5\;\wedge\;p^{\text{image}}_{\text{valid}}>p^{\text{LiDAR}}_{\text{valid}}\\ \mathbf{p}^{\text{LiDAR}},&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} (26)

with 𝐩source=[pvalidsource,pobstsource]⊺\mathbf{p}^{\textsc{source}}=\bigl[p^{\textsc{source}}_{\text{valid}},\;p^{\textsc{source}}_{\text{obst}}\bigr]^{\intercal}, source∈{comb,image,LiDAR}\textsc{source}\in\{\text{comb},\text{image},\,\text{LiDAR}\}. The probability vector 𝐩comb\mathbf{p}^{\text{comb}} defines the final combined soft labels (our combined labels), which we use for supervision of obstacle semantics. Table 7 summarizes the hyperparameters used in the obstacle segmentation pipeline.

B.3 Occupancy World Model Loss Functions

We provide additional loss function details for the occupancy (ℒocc\mathcal{L}_{\text{occ}}) and obstacle segmentation (ℒseg\mathcal{L}_{\text{seg}}) loss: The occupancy loss is a binary cross-entropy loss summed across all query points:

ℒocc=−1|𝒬++𝒬−|​(∑𝐪∈𝒬−log⁡(1−fθ,occ​(𝐪))+∑𝐪∈𝒬+log⁡(fθ,occ​(𝐪))).\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{occ}}=-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Q^{+}}+\mathcal{Q^{-}}|}\left(\sum_{\mathbf{q}\in\mathcal{Q}^{-}}\log(1-f_{\theta,\text{occ}}(\mathbf{q}))+\sum_{\mathbf{q}\in\mathcal{Q}^{+}}\log(f_{\theta,\text{occ}}(\mathbf{q}))\right). (27)

The groundness probability loss is similarly defined as a soft focal loss function, weighted by the validity probability:

ℒseg=−1|𝒫sweep|∑𝐪∈𝒫sweeppvalidcomb​(𝐪)​(α​pgroundcomb​(𝐪)​(1−fθ,seg​(𝐪))γ​log⁡(fθ,seg​(𝐪))CLOSEOPEN+(1−α)​(1−pgroundcomb​(𝐪))​(fθ,seg​(𝐪))γ​log⁡(1−fθ,seg​(𝐪))).\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\text{seg}}=-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}_{\text{sweep}}|}&\sum_{\mathbf{q}\in\mathcal{P}_{\text{sweep}}}p^{\text{comb}}_{\text{valid}}(\mathbf{q})\Big(\alpha\,p^{\text{comb}}_{\text{ground}}(\mathbf{q})\big(1-f_{\theta,\text{seg}}(\mathbf{q})\big)^{\gamma}\log\!\big(f_{\theta,\text{seg}}(\mathbf{q})\big)\\ &+(1-\alpha)\big(1-p^{\text{comb}}_{\text{ground}}(\mathbf{q})\big)\big(f_{\theta,\text{seg}}(\mathbf{q})\big)^{\gamma}\log\!\big(1-f_{\theta,\text{seg}}(\mathbf{q})\big)\Big).\end{split} (28)

with α=0.25\alpha=0.25 and γ=2.0\gamma=2.0.

B.4 Training of Downstream Task

LiDAR Forecasting.

For LiDAR forecasting, we apply techniques from prior work [42, 1, 18]. We first train the occupancy world model fθf_{\theta}, followed by a training of a LiDAR forecasting header fψf_{\psi} with frozen occupancy parameters θ\theta and new parameters ψ\psi. This model is specifically trained to predict the expected depth of a LiDAR for the task of lidar forecasting. We use an L1L_{1} loss to supervise the depth of the model under the assumption of previous works that the direction of the LiDAR ray can be assumed to be known, and that our goal is to render where the ray terminates. Therefore, given a set of LiDAR rays 𝒫ray\mathcal{P}_{\text{ray}} with LiDAR ray returns 𝐥\mathbf{l} we wish to sample, we formulate the loss as:

ℒlidar=1|𝒫ray|​∑𝐥∈𝒫ray|fψ​(fθ,occ​(𝐥))−∥𝐥∥2|.\mathcal{L}_{\text{lidar}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}_{\text{ray}}|}\sum_{\mathbf{l}\in\mathcal{P}_{\text{ray}}}\left|f_{\psi}(f_{\theta,\text{occ}}(\mathbf{l}))-\lVert\mathbf{l}\rVert_{2}\right|. (29)

In practice, during training we randomly sample 50 LiDAR rays, then further sample 2000 points per ray at 0.1m resolution to calculate our LiDAR forecasting loss.

BEV/ 3D Supervised Semantic Occupancy.

For supervised occupancy training, we simply use binary cross entropy to train the model using the rasterized box labels of the objects of interest. For the sake of evaluating how well the model forecasts the occupancy of fast moving objects, we focus on supervising exclusively on the vehicle class. Therefore, for a set of points 𝒰\mathcal{U} uniformly sampled in 2D BEV (LRR) or 3D (AV2) over the region of interest, and a label function Ras​(𝐪)\text{Ras}(\mathbf{q}) that returns 1 if the query point lies within a bounding box and 0 if not, with the loss function defined in Equation 27.

B.5 Training Hyperparameters

We train TriO on 16 GPUs using the AdamW optimizer with a cosine learning rate schedule. The learning rate begins at 8.0×10−58.0\times 10^{-5} and follows a 1,000-iteration warmup period to reach a peak of 8.0×10−48.0\times 10^{-4}. We set N=|𝒬+|=|𝒬−|=7500N=|\mathcal{Q}^{+}|=|\mathcal{Q}^{-}|=7500, |𝒫sweep|=10000|\mathcal{P}_{\text{sweep}}|=10000, and |ℛclean|=2000|\mathcal{R}_{\text{clean}}|=2000, with loss weights configured as λ1=1500,λ2=10\lambda_{1}=1500,\lambda_{2}=10, and λ3=125\lambda_{3}=125. Note for a fair comparison, hyperparameters of baselines are also tuned.

B.6 Extended Discussion of Unsupervised Framing

Throughout this paper, we use unsupervised to denote that TriO’s training pipeline requires no human-provided annotations (e.g., bounding boxes, semantic labels, or text prompts). The pre-trained model used for pseudo-label generation (Metric3Dv2 [32]) was supervised on geometric properties (depth and normals), which can be derived from LiDAR and reconstructions. Nevertheless, some datasets (e.g., [14]) used by [32] (see Tab. 5 in the reference) contain further human-in-the-loop work like CAD model alignment; hence, we restrict our unsupervised claim to TriO’s own training pipeline and not the entire system.

C Experimental Setup

In this section we provide additional details for our experimental setup on Argoverse 2 (AV2) [94], Spotting the Unexpected (STU) [67] and the unreleased dataset Long Range Radar (LRR).

C.1 Occupancy World Model Pre-training (AV2/LRR)

AV2 is a dataset collected in six cities in the United States, especially mined for interesting urban scenarios. We use the official split with 750 train and 150 val sequences. Each sequence spans 15 s15\text{\,}\mathrm{s} with 150 frames. We train TriO on a ROI of [−100,150][-100,150]m in the xx dimension [−100,100][-100,100] in the y dimension and [−4.5,4.5][-4.5,4.5]m in zz dimension. For generating the segmentation labels, we use all eight cameras of the camera rig ([94]). We train our model with the front left and front right cameras (OPENNC=2)N_{\text{C}}=2) for memory efficiency and use one LiDAR (NL=1N_{\text{L}}=1). We use H=3.0 sH=$3.0\text{\,}\mathrm{s}$ of past data sampled at 5Hz and pre-train to predict T=3.0 sT=$3.0\text{\,}\mathrm{s}$ into the future. We also ablated using four cameras (D.1), which led to slight performance gains.

LRR is a dataset with urban and highway driving with 2280 sequences each 20 seconds long, whereas we use 19 sequences for evaluation. TriO uses NC=5N_{\text{C}}=5 cameras, NL=6N_{\text{L}}=6 LiDAR and NR=4N_{\text{R}}=4 RADAR. We use H=0.5 sH=$0.5\text{\,}\mathrm{s}$ of past data sampled at 10 Hz and pre-train with to predict T=1.5 sT=$1.5\text{\,}\mathrm{s}$ into the future. We use an ROI of [−50,350][-50,350] m on the xx dimension [−50,50][-50,50] on the y dimension and [−2,4][-2,4] m in zz dimension.

C.2 Zero-Shot Anything Perception Evaluation (STU)

We evaluate zero-shot obstacle segmentation on long-tail obstacles using the Spotting the Unexpected (STU) dataset, where we use one LiDAR (NL=1N_{\text{L}}=1) and one front camera (NC=1N_{\text{C}}=1) featuring sensor characteristics that differ from those on AV2. The STU dataset is split into three parts: a train set, a validation set, and a non-public test set. The train set consists of two sequences and represents naturalistic driving data with fully labeled scenes. The validation set contains 19 sequences and features a variety of unexpected obstacles placed in the road, but does not contain labels for the ground. We combine the train and validation sets into a single dataset for our evaluations in the following manner: first we retain only points with negative (ground) labels from the train set, second we retain only points with positive (obstacle) labels from the validation set. This combined set is only used for evaluation and not for training or fine-tuning the models trained on AV2. The combination allows for an evaluation focused on how well rare obstacles can be segmented from the road.

Next we detail pre-processing steps used in our evaluation process. First, labeled LiDAR points are filtered to the height range z∈[−3,5]z\in[-3,5] m and to those projecting into the front camera’s field of view via pinhole projection with the provided intrinsics, extrinsics, and distortion parameters. For the implicit world model evaluations (TriO), each LiDAR point 𝐥=(lx,ly,lz)\mathbf{l}=(l_{x},l_{y},l_{z}) is augmented with a zero timestamp to form a query point 𝐪=(lx,ly,lz,lt=0)\mathbf{q}=(l_{x},l_{y},l_{z},l_{t}{=}0). Then, the decoder is queried with these LiDAR points to obtain predictions for occupancy and groundness. Points with predicted occupancy of less than 0.5 are assigned to ground. For image-based baselines, obstacle segmentation prediction is obtained by projecting LiDAR points onto the segmentation image associated with the front camera. For image methods with binarized outputs, ignore/invalid classifications are mapped to ground. For image methods with probabilistic outputs, the valid probability channel is ignored when determining the pixel label (leaving only pobstimagep^{\text{image}}_{\text{obst}} and pgroundimagep^{\text{image}}_{\text{ground}} ). Thus, we produce a set of predictions and their associated labels that can be used for evaluation of both implicit models and image space models.

Metrics.

Given these predictions and their associated labels, a precision–recall curve is computed over the combined dataset. The operating-point threshold is selected to maximize the F1F_{1} score. All metrics requiring an operating point are reported using this optimal threshold. Models that output already binarized have their binarized output used directly. We report four metrics: (i) mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) (ii) F1F_{1} score; (iii) recall; and (iv) Average Precision (AP).

  • •

    mIoU [%\%]: This metric is the mean Intersection over Union, and represents the number of points that are correctly predicted to be the desired class, divided by the union of the prediction and the labels for said class. This is averaged over the two classes equally and is generally a standard metric for semantic occupancy [91].

  • •

    F1 [%\%]: This formally represents the harmonic mean over precision and recall. It represents how well the model can balance both of these metrics at a single optimal operating point. This metric is more suitable for evaluating the segmentation pseudo-labels than other metrics such as mean average precision, due to the fact that they evaluate at a single operating point, and therefore do not unfairly advantage soft metrics that return the probability of each class.

  • •

    Recall [%\%]: Recall tracks the proportion of ground-truth obstacle points that are correctly classified as obstacle points. This is important for evaluating the safety of autonomous driving systems, as missing even a single obstacle could lead to a critical failure of the overall system.

  • •

    AP[%\%]: Average Precision represents the area under the precision recall curve, and is often used to determine how well a model is able to interplay between true positives, false positives, and false negatives. However, the precision recall curve is computed over a series of different thresholds, and therefore this metric is designed with continuous probability models in mind. As a result, we only use this metric on our occupancy baselines, where a direct comparison is fair.

Baselines

We benchmark against several state-of-the-art open-vocabulary segmentation methods: GroundedSAM [76] employs an open-set object detector, Grounding DINO [58], with various text prompts to query SAM [45]. Similarly, we introduce an OWLv2+SAM baseline that replaces the Grounding DINO detector with OWLv2 [64]. These methods follow a detect-then-segment paradigm. Conversely, we also evaluate segment-then-classify approaches, where the image is first partitioned into masks which are subsequently classified. We utilize the state-of-the-art MaskCLIP++ [99] framework, which we combine with various mask predictors. Specifically, we evaluate mask predictors from FC-CLIP [97] and MAFT+ [38] and SAM. We also compare against more heuristic-based ground segmentation models, such as Patchwork++ [47], which uses estimated LiDAR elevation to compare against what is and what isn’t ground.

For the second set of experiments, we also train TriO’s segmentation objective (ℒseg\mathcal{L}_{\text{seg}}) using each of the pseudo-labels from the baselines. The goal is to determine how well this information can be distilled into a downstream world model, and in turn how well this model generalizes when evaluated on a different domain. Notably, our model under GroundedSAM supervision can be viewed as an extension of the recent work QueryOcc+ [54], albeit with a distinct architecture and additional LiDAR input. Finally, we also add baselines training the LiDAR-only based models DIO [18] and UnO [1] with the pseudo-labels from our method (ISL, CSL).

Text Prompts.

For all open-vocabulary methods, we utilize a consistent set of prompts for ground (𝒫ground\mathcal{P}_{\text{ground}}) and obstacle (𝒫obst\mathcal{P}_{\text{obst}}) classes based on [69]. Simply put, we start with those prompts and then map them to either the obstacle or the ground class as shown in Table 8. Following common practices, the baselines also wrap each text prompt into a full sentence, resulting in prompts like a photo of a pedestrian. The MaskCLIP++ (MCPP) baselines first generate a set of mask, which are later classified. To avoid assigning regions like the sky to either ground or obstacle, we prompt those models additionally with the prompt sky and map this later to an ignore class, which enables a more fair comparison.

Finally, recognizing that a closed-set of predefined prompts are inherently limited and risks omitting rare object classes, to establish an upper bound for open-vocabulary performance, we include an (Oracle) variant where scenes are manually inspected and specific unknown object classes are appended to 𝒫obstacle\mathcal{P}_{\text{obstacle}}. We show these prompts in Table 9.

C.3 LiDAR Forecasting (AV2)

Following the Argoverse 2 leaderboard, we report the following four metrics using the same evaluation protocol:

  • •

    L1 [ m\text{\,}\mathrm{m}] The average absolute error between the depth predicted by the occupancy model and the ground truth LiDAR ray depth. This is the primary metric for the AV2 leaderboard rankings.

  • •

    AbsRel [%\%] The absolute error of the LiDAR ray normalized by the ground truth depth.

  • •

    CD [ m2$\text{\,}\mathrm{m}$^{2}]: The Chamfer Distance between the predicted LiDAR point cloud and the ground truth. It is defined as the mean squared distance from every point in the predicted point cloud to its nearest neighbor in the true point cloud.

  • •

    NFCD [ m2$\text{\,}\mathrm{m}$^{2}]: The Near Field Chamfer Distance, which measures the Chamfer distance between the predicted and ground truth point clouds within a restricted 70m×\times 70m range.

C.4 Downstream Occupancy Fine-tuning (AV2/LRR)

On AV2, the evaluation ROI is same as training except only 25m to the sides due to memory constraints and at a resolution of 0.5 m0.5\text{\,}\mathrm{m} every 0.1 s0.1\text{\,}\mathrm{s}. LRR uses the same evaluation ROI (x,y)(x,y) as described in Section C.1. We evaluate on a grid of query points with resolution 0.3125 m0.3125\text{\,}\mathrm{m} every 0.3 s0.3\text{\,}\mathrm{s}.

Metrics.

The fine-tuning experiments for BEV/3D semantic occupancy/flow forecasting use the following metrics:

  • •

    mAP [%\%]: This mean average precision metric is the average area under the precision recall curve when the predicted occupancy is evaluated against the rasterized bounding box labels. This can be done in both 2D BEV and in 3D.

  • •

    IoU [%\%]: Soft Intersection Over Union is a metric originally proposed by [62] as a more calibrated soft evaluation method for occupancy. It is the probabilistic equivalent of IoU, previously introduced.

  • •

    EPE [%\%]: End point error represents the L2L_{2} distance between the ground truth flow vector, and the predicted flow vector. This can be computed in 2D for 2D BEV models, and in 3D.

D Additional Experiments

D.1 Quantitative Results

Runtime and Memory.

In Table 10, we provide the runtime and memory usage for TriO and the baselines on an NVIDIA RTX 5000 GPU. We also report the number of parameters for each method. We distinguish between two settings: The first setting (eval) is evaluated on a full grid of query points (x,y,t)(x,y,t), totaling 2,048,000 points; this setting is also used to compute our metrics. We observe that UnO and DIO achieve lower runtime and memory usage, which can be attributed to the addition of the new camera and RADAR sensors in TriO. Specifically, the camera encoding contributes to an increased parameter count, motivating the need for more efficient architectures in future work. In the second setting, we query the model with 20,000 points and measure the resulting runtime and memory. This is motivated by the number of query points used by a state-of-the-art planner, as reported by QuAD [6]. We observe a significant reduction in runtime across all methods when transitioning from the grid (eval: 2,048k) to the planner (20k) query setting. Notably, TriO (no camera) achieves the best runtime, rendering the method real-time capable.

Additional Camera Ablations

Tab. 11 shows marginal gains from 4 cameras on AV2 in occupancy, flow, and LiDAR metrics. However, these were not enough to justify the added cost during our main experiments, which aligns with our no-camera ablations in the main paper.

Expanding on our no camera ablation study in the main paper on LRR, we find camera inputs increases occupancy performance at range lending to the idea that camera features are more dense than other sensor modalities such as LiDAR at these distances. Howeve, since we only pass in one timestep of camera data as input to the model, we hypothesize this may be responsible for the slight regression in flow estimation since a single timestep of camera is insufficient to estimate flow by itself. The improvement in flow in AV2, contrasting with the decline seen in the LRR "no-camera" ablation, is likely because AV2 (urban) contains significantly more static vehicles. In contrast, LRR (highway/urban) includes many high-velocity objects for which single-frame camera input is less informative. Furthermore, LiDAR provides a dominant signal for geometric labels (occupancy, obstacle segmentation) except at long range, where sparsity increases; this aligns with the observed occupancy improvements at range when incorporating camera data. Future work could explore camera pre-training to better leverage multi-modal features.

Unsupervised Flow Estimation

In Tab. 12, we compare the unsupervised flow estimation of TriO against that of DIO [18], which uses a warping consistency loss. We observe that our method, directly supervised with RADAR, provides the best unsupervised flow estimation. We find that DIO only learns a minimal amount of flow on the surface of objects, leaving the occupancy in the interior stationary. This is also reflected in the EPE (static) metric, where DIO performs well due to predicting zero flow. As a result, our RADAR supervised flow results in significantly more accurate predictions, especially for dynamic obstacles as shown by the EPE (dynamic).

Breakdown of AV2 Prediction Metrics

Tab. 13 shows a metrics breakdown in near and far field. We contacted the leaderboard creators and confirmed the published L1 and AbsRel metrics are implicitly near field. Tab. 13 shows our re-implemented UnO and DIO baselines, have slightly different metrics (better L1, worse CD) than the results from the leaderboard in the main paper, but in general we do better close by and worse at range.

Sensitivity Analysis

Fig. 8 shows the current 0.5 threshold is a good balance between recall and F1 score. The method is robust balance across all metrics; performance only degrades at extreme values. We also perform loss sensitivity analysis on LRR. Scaling each loss weight by 4×4\times and 0.25×0.25\times shows that TriO is robust to this, with min/max deviations of 0.1/0.2%0.1/0.2\% AP, 0.0/0.4%0.0/0.4\% SoftIoU, 0.03/0.440.03/0.44 m EPE.

D.2 Qualitative Results

We provide additional qualitative visualizations to highlight different aspects of TriO and the baselines. Figures 10 and 11 show diverse AV2 scenes, illustrating the model’s generalization across a wide range of scenarios and obstacle types, including VRUs, construction vehicles, animals, infrastructure, and challenging weather conditions like snow.

Figures 12 and 13 compare our pseudo-labels against several open-vocabulary VLM baselines on a broad range of uncommon obstacles, emphasizing both the strong generalization of our model and representative failure cases of current state-of-the-art VLMs, even when supplied with ’ground-truth’ text prompts (Oracle).

Figures 14 and 15 present additional zero-shot results of our model, trained on AV2, via roll-outs on STU that showcase obstacle segmentation for rare objects. In addition Figure 16 shows an AV2 rollout containing a vulnerable road user on a scooter. Figure 17 visualizes forecasted LiDAR vs ground-truth LiDAR on a challenging scenario with different traffic participants. Figures 18 and 19 summarize typical failure modes on AV2 and STU, respectively.

Meanwhile, Figure 20 showcase how our model successfully extends to edge cases such as speed bumps and hilly roads.

E Extended Limitations and Future Work

For obstacle segmentation pseudo-labels, we use a late-fusion approach that combines image- and LiDAR-based segmentation, where pseudo-labels are first generated independently for each modality. Since both segmentation approaches rely primarily on surface normals, future work could explore unified early-fusion methods such as [41]. Although including cameras as an input improves long-range occupancy performance, it also increases runtime and memory usage. Future work should therefore investigate more efficient camera encoding approaches.

While TriO also generalizes to other weather conditions, for example as shown in Figure 10, we sometimes observe false-positive occupancy and obstacle segmentation predictions caused by snow and exhaust (Figure 18). Incorporating more occupancy self-supervision from cameras and RADAR could help mitigate these failures. We acknowledge that open-loop metrics may not fully capture final closed-loop driving performance. Although this is beyond the scope of the present paper, we are interested in studying how TriO can be used directly in downstream motion planning tasks, since the ability to detect and avoid rarely seen objects is vital for self-driving.

Another area for future work is improving upon the flow representation. Forecasted occupancy warped via 3D flow (Fig. 9 a) reveals inconsistencies between both. While RADAR flow is a strong pretraining signal (Tab. 3) outperforming consistency-baselines (Tab. 6, Supp.), it is insufficient for standalone metric flow. TriO resolves 3D flow from 1D radial Doppler with spatially and temporally diverse measurements: Multiple RADAR sensors capture distinct radial components of the same velocity vector from different viewpoints, resolving the full 3D flow via geometric triangulation. A single object can also yield multiple returns across its spatial extent, and we supervise with future sensor frames, making learning only radial flow non-trivial. We hypothesize that the location invariance in the CNN backbone also helps. However, tangential failures (Fig. 9 b) persist, likely due to highway motion biases.
